ety.text: Anglo-Norman sausichebor. Middle English sawsiche English sausage From late Middle English sawsiche, from Anglo-Norman sausiche (compare Norman saûciche), from Late Latin salsīcia (compare Sicilian sausizza, Spanish salchicha, Italian salsiccia), feminine of salsīcius (“seasoned with salt”), derivative of Latin salsus (“salted”), from sal (“salt”). More at salt. Doublet of saucisse. See also Sicilian sausizza. Displaced native Old English mearh.

senses.d: A food made of ground meat (or meat substitute) and seasoning, packed in a section of the animal's intestine, or in a similarly cylindrical shaped synthetic casing.
An individual item of this food.
A sausage-shaped thing.
A penis.
A term of endearment.
A saucisse.
A dachshund; sausage dog.
To squeeze (something) tightly into in a rolled or sausage-like form.
ex: He leapt to his feet, carefully sausaged his screwdrivers in a roll beneath his arm and turned to reach into the box.
In the top drawer were neatly piled thermals and socks sausaged into pairs.

senses.d: To squeeze (something) into something tightly fitting.
ex: He is sausaged into several overcoats and wears a brown macintosh under which he holds a roll of parchment.
The second Mrs. Teague wore a baby blue tank top and too-tight white shorts that sausaged her hips.

senses.d: To fit snugly into.
ex: Dressing in a flash, she sausaged on her skinny jeans and sleeveless camo top with peek-a-boo sides for boob aficionados.

senses.d: To make into sausage.
ex: At butchering time, they kept three pigs for their own use, smoking, brining, and sausaging the meat, and trying the lard.
The fresh meat was sausaged into the tripes of pig and deer and ox, because the time for salting was not yet come.

senses.d: To make sausage-like, especially to give the appearance of barely fitting into the casing or skin.
To form a sausage-like shape, with a non-uniform cross section.

grp.label: a food made of minced meat packed into a tubular casing

PIE word *sḗh₂l From Middle English sauce, from Old French sause, from Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), past participle of saliō (“to salt”), from sal. Doublet of salsa. For the meaning development compare Ancient Greek ἥδυσμα (hḗdusma) ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (whence also English sweet).

senses.d: Vitality; capability or talent.
ex: It's over for that guy. He lost the sauce.

senses.d: Anabolic steroids.

Vegetables.

senses.d: Any garden vegetables eaten with meat.
To add sauce to; to season.
To cause to relish anything, as if with a sauce; to tickle or gratify, as the palate; to please; to stimulate.
ex: Earth, yield me roots; / Who seeks for better of thee, sauce his palate / With thy most operant poison!
Meales, uſually ſavvced vvith a healthfull hunger, vvherein no incocted Crudities oppreſſe Nature, and cheriſh diſeaſe: […]

senses.d: To make poignant; to give zest, flavour or interest to; to set off; to vary and render attractive.
ex: Then fell she to sauce her desires with threatenings.

senses.d: To treat with bitter, pert, or tart language; to be impudent or saucy to.
ex: I'll sauce her with bitter words.

senses.d: To send or hand over.
